questions.q: Which of these is **seasonality** in monthly air-conditioner sales?
options: Sales fell during a two-year recession
Sales peak every May and dip every December
Sales spiked once after a viral social-media post
Sales have grown steadily over ten years
questions.why: Seasonality repeats at a fixed, known interval (here 12 months). A recession is a cycle of irregular length; a one-off spike is an event to model separately; steady growth is trend.

questions.q: In a sales series, December is about 30% above trend every year, and the absolute size of the December peak grows as the business grows. Which decomposition fits?
questions.why: When seasonal swings scale with the level, the effect is a percentage, so the model is multiplicative (or additive on the logs). Additive assumes a fixed amount every year. Differencing removes components rather than describing them.

questions.q: Trend sales are ₹80 lakh a month and April's multiplicative seasonal factor is 1.25. If the trend grows to ₹160 lakh, what is the forecast for April?
questions.why: Multiplicative: 160 × 1.25 = ₹200 lakh. ₹180 lakh adds today's fixed April uplift of ₹20 lakh, which is what an additive model would wrongly do, under-forecasting the peak.

questions.q: A series alternates 1, 3, 1, 3, 1, 3. What is its lag-1 autocorrelation?
questions.why: Mean = 2, deviations −1, +1, −1, +1, −1, +1, sum of squares 6. The five lag-1 products are each −1, so r₁ = −5 / 6 = −0.83. It is not exactly −1 because only five pairs overlap in a series of six.

questions.q: The ACF of monthly revenue starts near 1 at lag 1 and decays very slowly over 24 lags. What does that suggest?
options: The series is not stationary (it has a trend), so it should be differenced before fitting a model such as ARIMA
questions.why: A very slowly decaying ACF is the signature of a trending, non-stationary series: every value resembles its neighbours because the level keeps drifting. Seasonality would show as spikes at 12 and 24, and white noise as near-zero autocorrelation at all lags.

questions.q: What does **seasonal differencing** of monthly data, y_t − y_{t−12}, remove?
options: Nothing; it only shifts the series
A stable seasonal pattern (and part of the trend), by comparing each month with the same month last year
questions.why: Subtracting the same month last year cancels a seasonal pattern that repeats each year; ordinary differencing (y_t − y_{t−1}) removes trend. You should still check the differenced series for stationarity.

questions.q: After decomposing two years of daily sales with a yearly seasonal component, the residual ACF shows clear spikes at lags 7, 14 and 21. What does this mean?
options: The decomposition is good; residuals always have some spikes
A weekly pattern has been missed: the residuals still contain predictable structure, so add a 7-day seasonal component
The trend estimate is too smooth
questions.why: Good residuals look random, with no ACF spikes. Spikes at 7 and its multiples are the fingerprint of weekly seasonality that the yearly component cannot capture. Leaving it in the residuals throws away forecastable signal.

questions.q: In an interview: "What does it mean for a series to be stationary, and why does ARIMA care?"
options: Its average level, spread and autocorrelation pattern stay the same over time; ARIMA's coefficients describe a stable relationship with the past, which only makes sense if the series is stable, hence differencing first
It has been decomposed into components
questions.why: Stationary means the series behaves the same way throughout its history, not that it is constant. A growing sales series is not stationary, but its month-to-month changes often are, which is why ARIMA differences d times. Decomposition separates components; it does not make a series stationary by itself.
